5.112.m: Śambhu said: / ‘Now I will tell another supreme narrative about a woman: / what was attained by the daughter of Devarāta through the recitation of the [Lord's] name.
The daughter of Devarāta was a young girl named Kalā, exceedingly beautiful; / she was the wife of the wise Śoṇa, son of Dhanañjaya.
Both of them, self-restrained, always solely intent on dharma, auspicious, / found a treasure; then the two went to bathe in the Gaṅgā.
Having gone to the riverbank fallen into the current to fetch clay, / taking a clod of earth from the bank, they saw a great jar,
made of silver, with a stone placed on top. Then Śoṇa spoke / this word to his beloved: ‘How is this to be done? What indeed should be done for our benefit?’
The wife said: / ‘One should not undertake any action by relying on a woman's opinion; / nor should one practice any secret or unpleasant thing with a woman.
If wealth should fall into view in the presence of a woman, / one should deceive that woman with words such as these:
“We must not look at it; what indeed is lying there? / If it is wealth, it must not be looked upon, [lest] injury occur in the future.
If it has been known by another, whence would there be certainty of knowledge? / And if it has not been seen now, someone may be staying there secretly.
If there is no concealment, someone may be present there by illusion. / If it is not by illusion of men, a guardian of the site (kṣetrapāla) might be stationed there.
If not [a kṣetrapāla], Bhairava is present here, or a Brahmarākṣasa resides [here]. / Even if he is not there, a great spell of kings will be there.
And if the king does not know, litigation and the like could arise; / if it is kept secret, danger from thieves will arise.
Great misfortune will befall you, even though you are not negligent. / Generally, the desire for pleasures arises in wealthy men;
and from one pleasure comes the desire for another pleasure, which destroys all religious observance. / If a woman knows that her own [husband] has attained such an emotional state,
the woman attains independence, revealing herself out of anger; / in anger she seeks confidence, and then the fault previously mentioned occurs.
In one who trusts, there is intimacy, or absence from home, or distraction of mind; / from intimacy various activities arise in women.
Seeing any young man, affection might arise; / through affection union arises, and from union sexual intercourse.
When intercourse occurs constantly, an inner breach of trust occurs: / [she thinks,] “Either I was enjoyed by you before, and now I am enjoyed [again];
what expectation do you have now, or in whom is there affection? / What clever, deeply affectionate woman would turn away from a man?”
Or she speaks a word to him: “If you tell me today, / I will say everything just so; the word cannot be spoken otherwise.”
And having thus attained boldness, and under an altered form, / taking whatever wealth [there is], she might behave independently.
Having slain [the husband] and taken the wealth, she will bring ruin. / Or, when her husband dies first, she will not enter the fire,
[thinking,] “In widowhood all this wealth will belong to me for dharma.” / Having determined this in her mind, when widowhood arrives,
approaching the vulva-altar by day or by night, / going to a solitary place and baring her vulva of its cloth,
the faithful wife, placing her hands on her pudenda, spoke this word out of grief: / “What deformity was done by you, O vulva? What sin did you embrace?
Or what sin of the penis [occurred] because of its entering inside you? / And what sin was committed by the agent by omitting the service of one such as me?”
Moreover, when an itch arises, she would insert her finger; / having performed strange actions because of the notion of an itch thereafter,
rubbing it with both hands, striking it, and opening it, / repeatedly shaking her feet, open-mouthed, exceedingly sorrowful,
then embracing the bedpost as if pressing her breasts against her beloved; / then, in the state of a disturbed mind, she becomes completely depraved.
Or else, dwelling in the city of the fire-god, what vegetable was bought / having depended upon in the house at night, at twilight, and in the alleys,
assuming another disguise, she is enjoyed by whoever [comes along]; / or else, apprehensive because of the power of gossip, she would bring a suitable [man].
And going to an unknown house, she would certainly enjoy herself.” / If wealth is obtained in the presence of a woman, this is what is expected.
Therefore, even with me there is no need for your deliberation.’ / Śoṇa said: ‘It is so, there is no doubt. Go, stand at a distance.
Having paused for the sake of discharging stool and urine, I will come after this.’ / When she had gone, Śoṇa prepared pieces of cloth.
Then, in each piece [of cloth], he took much wealth; / and having made [holes] knee-deep here and there in the sand,
having thrown in the wealth and filled [the holes], he made feces over them; / and the jar, the container of the cloths, he cast away somewhere.
Making everything appear as if unnoticed, the sage proceeded to bathe. / His wife, having then bathed and worshipped Pārvatī,
Told by her husband, "Go," that virtuous wife returned to her own house. / Learning that she was all alone, a rākṣasa named Mārīca,
assuming the form of her husband, spoke thus to Kalā: / Mārīca said: / "On the bank of the Saptagodāvarī, holy and destroying sins,
is the place called Drākṣārāma, where Bhīma resides in person, / bestowing enjoyment and liberation upon mortals, destroying sins at mere remembrance.
Let us both go there at once; do you come forth, O beautiful one!" / Kalā said: / "Just now you set out for the ceremonial bath and have not performed it.
How is it that you say such a thing that was never mentioned before? / The wise consider an alteration of one's nature to be an omen of calamity."
Mārīca said: / "Not opposing one's husband is declared to be the duty of women. / Tell me quickly whether you oppose or agree with me!"
Falling silent, that virtuous woman, thinking only, 'He is my husband,' / went out with him, and the young woman arrived in the midst of a forest.
Then [she said]: "This is midday; let the daily rites be performed!" / Hearing her words, the rākṣasa [said]: "There is no place here for religious observances.
We must go wherever there is one; therefore let us move on from here." / Having gone some distance and seeing a cave as well as a lake, [he said]:
"This is indeed a place for me to stay; my bath must be taken now, my dear." / Having spoken thus, he bathed in the lake, and after arranging a meal of fruit,
when the time for eating arrived, Kalā meditated upon Umā and Śiva. / 'Is this my husband or not?' she wondered, absorbed in meditation.
Then, having determined through meditation that he was an imposter, that devoted wife, / terrified, with deeply lowered face, her countenance filled with tears,
said, "A wretched calamity has befallen me!" and fell to the ground. / Seeing her weeping, the rākṣasa, bent on evil,
began to assault her. But as she resisted this assault, / and while the rākṣasa attempted to use force,
[the goddess] made her body from knees to navel turn into stone; / her garment became like rock. Seeing her thus,
"In this manner I shall kill her, and hereafter I shall devour her!" / Having said this and brandished his sword, he began to cut off her head.
"I am Kalā; my husband, learning of this, will lay a curse on you! Do not strike!" / No sooner were these words spoken than the rākṣasa severed her head.
When she had met an untimely death, Śaiva messengers arrived, / adorned with wondrous ornaments, bearing all weapons, auspicious.
Placing her on an aerial chariot, they went to the world of Śiva. / Having honored with joy the arrived woman,
who was bowed at her feet and pure, Umā, the Daughter of the Mountain, spoke these words: / "I am pleased with your devotion to your husband; I grant you your heart's desire."
Kalā said: / "Grant me the status of a handmaiden; your lotus feet are dear to me. / What need have I of many other boons to request?" "Let it be so," said Śivā.
She, a treasure of arts, was then worshipped by the wives of Indra and the others. / In the meantime, the sage Śoṇa returned to his home.
Not seeing his wife there, he absorbed himself in the yoga of meditation. / [He saw] that she had been carried off by the demon, died, and reached the realm of Śiva before Umā;
with his eye of wisdom he also saw that she had received a boon from Umā. / Somewhat sorrowful, meditating for a long time, the sage then turned back
and went to his father-in-law, Devarāta, the lord of sages. / Having reported everything, he went together with him to the sage Viśvāmitra.
Having reported that to Vasiṣṭha, Vasiṣṭha too addressed those sages: / "Having first gone to Kailāsa and seen the god Maheśvara,
and having obtained permission from Śiva, let us go to Pārvatī's dwelling, / and having reported everything to the goddess, let us explain the matter as it truly is."
Saying, "So be it," the excellent sages, having gone to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara, / and bowed to the Lord of Gods, were honored by Vīrabhadra.
They announced this: "Śoṇa's wife has been abducted." / Śiva spoke to those leaders of sages: "This has indeed been known by me.
Her death was untimely; a life-span of a hundred years still remained. / And for those who meet an untimely death, there is restoration of life.
She was to bear ten heroic sons, and was endowed with beauty and good fortune; / having resolved this, O twice-born, you have come here.
All this is certainly determined for those who have gone to the world of Yama; / but for those who have gone to my world, there is no other recourse.
My name was uttered by her earlier at the departure of her breath; / by that, the decree of Yama was erased; how can there be a determination of life-span?
Or rather, report everything completely to the Mountain's Daughter." / Then those twice-born went to see the feet of Pārvatī.
Having bowed to the Mother, they all—with Viśvāmitra as spokesman—said this: / "Having protected the poor, helpless, emaciated wife and the children whose father was lost,
O Mother, you were always in the past the granter of desires. / This Kalā is indeed my granddaughter; having propitiated you, she obtained
this Śoṇa as her husband, O Mother; this is indeed the fruit of your worship. / If by penance, O Goddess Aparṇā, or by charity,
or by vows and fasts, that Kalā can be obtained by me; / I desire to eat food served by her—how then [can that be]?"
Pārvatī said: / "Whatever kind of wife is desired, such a one shall be given by me; / I cannot give her up, or what do you think, O sage?"
Viśvāmitra said: / "Thinking 'You are the Mother,' I have spoken without hesitation; / this sage Śoṇa, O Mother, will make his plea to you."
Śoṇa said: / "My love is extremely intense toward that very wife; / let that same woman be given as my wife, otherwise death will be mine."
Pārvatī said: / "Wife and husband should be equal; an unequal pair is condemned. / She is not suited to you; I shall give one who is suited.
And I will not release one who has reached my abode and cast off her mortal body." / Śoṇa said: / "If this wife is not given to me, who am dear to you,
then grant the highest boon: kingship and devotion to Maheśvara!" / Saying, "This shall indeed be so," she then spoke to the sages:
"You must dine here for three days. / On every Monday, for the gratification of the god Maheśa,
eight Brahmins, lords of sages, should always be fed. / According to one's desire, one may undertake this vow anywhere.
When a year is completed, one should cause to be made a silver image of the Lord, / measuring four niṣkas, or half of that.
A pair of fine white garments, two fly-whisks, fans, / wooden sandals, shoes, and an umbrella—all this should be bestowed upon a Brahmin.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's means, the wise man should dismiss the Brahmins. / He should perform this closing ceremony at the beginning and in the middle as well.
Day after day, worship should likewise be offered to Soma, the Supreme Self:
'We know that Supreme Person; we meditate upon Mahādeva; / may that Rudra impel us!'
This is the mantra for worship: / One should worship the god on a bare patch of ground, or else upon an image; / one should oneself eat only one meal a day, maintaining celibacy.
This is declared to be the auspicious Somavrata, which bestows gratification upon Śiva; / whatever woman or man performs it thus with devotion,
always follows Śaṅkara like a shadow. / Today Monday has arrived; eating is to take place after midday.
And you, all the sages, having performed the morning rites / and then the midday rite, are worthy to dine, O best of men!"
Hearing their mother's word, they said, "So be it," and bowed; / to perform their religious observance, they all went to the river Bhāgīrathī.
At noon having performed their midday rite at the confluence, / and having worshiped Viśveśa with the sixteen offerings,
they went to Pārvatī's house and bowed down to the goddess. / At the command of the mother of the worlds, the son of Śālaṅkāyana
arranged the services beginning with the washing of feet; / taking the fivefold perfume, he anointed those sages.
Whoever offers the fivefold perfume attains a great kingdom; / becoming equal to the Five-Arrowed One, he becomes beloved of women.
Whoever indeed gives it to Viṣṇu becomes equal to Māra; / one with desire or one without desire who performs it [dwells] five years on Kailāsa,
endowed with all fragrances, an enjoyer, possessed of desired objects; / behaving according to his wish, he would then be born a king on earth.
Musk, sandalwood, camphor, and the two kinds of agallochum: / this is declared as the fivefold perfume, auspicious in all rites.
When the great-souled brāhmaṇas had been anointed with the fivefold perfume / and seated, there arrived an old, emaciated brāhmaṇa.
Attired like a madman, naked, worn out by old age, hastening, / bald, afflicted with wheezing and coughing, hiccuping incessantly, overcome by hunger,
dripping with saliva, with a beard and whiskers smeared with phlegm, bowed down, stumbling in his steps. / And [with him was] a woman sixteen years of age, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with beauty and grace, possessing a form superior to all in the world, / glancing this way and that at handsome men,
singing and dancing, and looking at that husband, laughing; / she tormented her aged husband: "Come quickly, you wretched emaciated man!
Holding your hand, old man, I am constantly miserable. / Ornaments, clothing, perfumes, garlands, and unguents,
laughter, singing, drinking, decoration, a lovely home, / and the abundance of all seasons exist solely for the increase of passion.
Of all desires, sensual pleasure alone is the ultimate aim. / All pleasures placed on one side, and sensual pleasure placed on the other:
weighed upon the scale, sensual pleasure is a hundred times greater! / Then what will one such as I, having obtained you, do?"
And speaking other words, holding her by the hand, / she spoke this in reply: "What can we do? Such is our destiny."
Do not kill me with harsh words, knowing me now to be like this." / Such a twice-born then went to Pārvatī's temple.
Not recognizing Girijā, he spoke these words: / The twice-born said: "Know me to have arrived here seeking food, as a guest, O sage!
Feed the brāhmaṇa who has arrived at the time of eating." / His wife spoke the word: "Where is a sage? This is only a woman!
Every utterance of a blind man is certainly like this." / Pārvatī said: "Having washed the two feet of this [guest], seat him on a seat."
She satisfied the twice-born with delicious food served on [a vessel] made of gold; / [she offered] nectar accompanied by an excellent jeweled cup to the expounder of the Veda.
Then having summoned Arundhatī, Ambikā had her serve the meal. / Kalā, Arundhatī, and the devoted wife Anasūyā,
adorned with garlands, perfumes, and unhusked barley grains, / at the word of Ambikā, served the food items of the six flavors separately.
As the brāhmaṇas were eating, he who had the form of a naked brāhmaṇa / consumed everything in an instant; the women were unable to supply [him].
Then the goddess Girijā herself set about giving [food]; / whatever was completely given, that twice-born ate up in an instant.
He wished to eat all that remained in the vessel, together with his beloved. / Thereupon Ambikā took it and gave it, saying: "May it be inexhaustible!"
Then he wished to eat with his left hand; thereupon the virtuous Satī / offered [it] to him, saying: "There too, may your food be inexhaustible!"
Then producing another hand, the best of the twice-born wished to eat; / in this manner, having made a thousand hands, the twice-born wished to eat.
Giving and giving repeatedly, the goddess was pleased and not angry. / Thinking, "It is impossible to alter her mind," the twice-born,
having washed his hands and feet, bearing the sweet fragrance placed upon his hands, / spoke this word to Pārvatī: "I am pleased, choose a boon!"
Pārvatī said: "If you are capable of granting me a boon, O best of brāhmaṇas, / what purpose do I have with a boon, since Śaṅkara is my husband?"
Then the brāhmaṇa said to the goddess: "What is Śaṅkara like? / Is he equal to you or not? He must be worthy of you, not otherwise.
Even being beloved by women, [possessing] beauty and cleverness, O auspicious woman— / otherwise, how could such a wife be under my control?"
Pārvatī said: "Having heard your wife's words and likewise your words, O twice-born, / this is a contradiction, O brāhmaṇa, or have you heard that which is discordant?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "I will dress your braided hair; mount onto my lap. / If your mind wavers, whence will come your devotion to your husband?"
Pārvatī said: "My vow, O best of the twice-born, is to mount only the lap of Śaṅkara." / Then, knowing that thought of Bhavānī, the Supreme Lord,
became sixteen years of age, with beautifully glossy bound hair, / with very glossy and beautiful eyes, with a body like cow's milk,
possessing the loveliness of tens of millions of Kandarpas, adorned with all ornaments, / with both arms outstretched on the shoulders of the woman standing at his side,
singing softly together with Umā, displaying his skill. / Then Śambhu, pulling that Pārvatī with his hand and smiling,

resting his two hands on the shoulders of the two women, singing, adorned with all ornaments, with serene eyes, / danced, his body overflowing with bliss, sung to by the chief of sages at the time of dusk.
Having meditated on such a Śiva, even through hundreds of millions of births / no sorrow arises for him, and joy arises perpetually.
Then, having been praised by the best of sages, and having transformed Hari into a woman, / that Pārvatī, pleased, spoke to the god wielding the Pināka bow:
Pārvatī said: "Why, adopting such a demeanor, did you come here? / Having turned Viṣṇu into a woman, why did you two not come in your natural forms?"
Śiva said: "In this vow, indeed, the feeding of a guest is auspicious. / I test the perfection of those in whom despondency does not arise.
If despondency arises, the vow is certainly imperfect—this is certain. / As many Mondays as arrive during a hundred years,
for so long [he dwells] in my city, O goddess, endowed with all enjoyments, / accompanied by his wife, sons, and kinsmen, having lived the lifespan stated in the Vedas.
Afterward, going to Vārāṇasī, having died, he will attain liberation." / Śambhu said: Then while the god stood there, the sages performed circumambulation three times,
made five prostrations, again performed circumambulation, / and falling like a staff, dismissed, they departed from there.
Then Śoṇa obtained a wife of fair limbs and blameless; / and the twice-born ruled the kingdom in Bhāratavarṣa with righteousness.
Devoted to Śiva, he enjoyed all human pleasures; / constantly dedicated to the worship of the gods, constantly honoring brāhmaṇas,
always giving, always sacrificing, always listening to the Purāṇa; / when he died, he went to the auspicious realm of the all-pervading Śaṅkara.
Śambhu said: The greatness of chanting the name has been proclaimed in this context, / destroying all sins of those devotees who hear it, O king.
It constantly grants all welfare, bestows an excellent wife and kingdom, is auspicious, / and grants devotion to Śiva; it should be kept secret and not proclaimed to just anyone."

5.113.m:
Glorious Rāma said:
"Auspicious [beings] bearing various forms are seen in the sky mounted on aerial chariots, / endowed with the fruit of all desires, having excellent wives, [each accompanied by] a hundred women,
revered at every step by thousands of men and women; / twenty women, delicate with beauty and charm, are singing.
One carries a spittoon; others have their arms devoted to flywhisks; / taking up a pair of palm-leaf fans, two women fan him.
He rests upon her lap, and another woman serves as a pillow; / the hand of one is held in his hands, and he is accompanied by many praisers.
His lotus face is blooming from various kinds of jesting; / and in each aerial chariot a moon-like radiance is seen.
In chariots containing hundreds of women, an auspicious lord is seen. / Are these doers of merit, O sage, or is this the māyā of Viṣṇu?"

Śambhu said:
"These indeed are meritorious brāhmaṇas who lived in the householder stage of life, / to whom a grant was given by Daśaratha.
Once, a thought occurred to the minds of those who were [dwelling] in my mind: / 'Just as here we are all happy and dependent on others,
and hundreds of men here depend upon us alone, / by what merit may we rejoice in all desires,
attended to by fine women, all endowed with the pleasures of kingship, / free from old age and death, and ever youthful?'
Reflecting thus, all the twice-born went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha. / Having honoured them when they arrived, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:

'For what purpose have you come? Speak quickly, O best of the twice-born.'
The twice-born said:
'We all desire to be carried in an aerial chariot,
endowed with all prosperity and moving at will; bring that about for us, O guru!' / Hearing that wish of theirs, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:
'The Purāṇa, which destroys sins, should always be heard, O brāhmaṇas; / dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are indeed seen therein.'
Saying 'So be it,' the sages then went to the sage skilled in the Purāṇas, / the foremost Aṅgiras, who was versed in all the scriptures,
knower of all Āgamas and Purāṇas, constantly engaged in good deeds. / Bowing down, they said this: 'Our lives have borne fruit;

we have achieved our aim, O brāhmaṇa, since you are seen in person, O sage.'
Aṅgiras said:
'Whatever the purpose for which you have arrived, that task I will accomplish.
You have assembled here wishing to hear the Purāṇa. / I shall proclaim to you the rite that destroys all sins,
bestowing all knowledge, divine, originating from realization of the truth, / granting devotion to Śiva, pleasing to the heart, granting devotion to Viṣṇu, auspicious,
granting knowledge of obtaining various celestial realms, bestowing lovely women, / [containing] various auspicious teachings, illuminating the techniques of love,
foremost in worldly enjoyment and liberation, illuminating the perception of injunctions, / recounting diverse devotions, proclaiming heroic deeds of devotion,
granting the rites of observances, consecrations, gifts, and the like, and the rules for worship with ashes. / The Padma Purāṇa, arising from the lotus of Brahmā, has been declared;
the description of the forms of the Pramathas was spoken by Maheśvara. / This was narrated elsewhere, but in the Padma Purāṇa,
Vasiṣṭha previously spoke this when asked by Dilīpa. / Listen to that, O best of sages; all knowledge will be yours.'
Then, at his word, the twice-born, eager to listen to the Purāṇa, / said to the sage: 'How should it now be heard, and having done what?'
He too explained everything: 'Hear the eternal duty: / having bowed to the knower of the Purāṇa, one should then offer him arghya and a seat.
Saying "Sit there," one should worship him with fragrant pastes and flowers, / and offer betel and abundant wealth according to one's means.
One should urge him: "O brāhmaṇa, recite the sacred Purāṇic narrative!" / Not mounting a cot, nor indeed a high seat,
one should listen seated upon a low seat, for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha. / Saying "Listen," the knower of the Purāṇa should recite this mantra:
"Salutation to Hari, then to Hara, to Gaṇeśa, and to Sarasvatī!" / Having bowed to the chosen deity, he is fit to recite the Purāṇa.
Every day [the recitation should last] half a yāma, or according to desire; / having heard thus until the conclusion of the reading, one should perform the requisite rites.
The listener should contemplate in silence, or listen in silence alone; / otherwise, Sarasvatī will be angry, and from her anger muteness will ensue.
Therefore, the listener to the Purāṇa should make an offering of betel and other gifts, / and provide a livelihood for the reciter according to his own means.
At the beginning of the Purāṇa, one should present garments, an upper cloth, / or fine cloth, or a pair of garments;
and a large, ornate, lovely, splendid, and soft seat; / or one should give gold, as well as cows, land, a house, and the like.
All this, O foremost of the twice-born, was previously declared by Śaṅkara / in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti to the sages and to the gods.'
Then all those sages, having bowed to him seated upon his seat / and each offering betel individually, stood eager to hear.
He too narrated the entire Purāṇa that bestows all [desires]; / up to the penultimate chapter, the best of the twice-born listened.

Dilīpa said:
'By means of an aerial chariot moving at will, abundant with all prosperity, / and accompanied by happiness on every side, the meritorious station is attained.'

Vasiṣṭha said:
'Not enough has been asked by you, O king! By other superior merits beyond this / they will sport [in heaven]; that merit will now be told:
having whitewashed the dwelling of Śiva completely with lime, / [one should provide] women rich in beauty and charm, adorned with all ornaments,
skilled in various melodious songs, expert in various dances, / four, eight, or six women making the sound of the mardala drum:
two controllers, two players of the āvajika drum, two striking with drumsticks and playing wind instruments, / four lasya dancers, and one delighted female singer,
and one or two who know fine singing and are celebrated as not too loud; / two for the percussion played with a stick, and six or eight remaining silent;
all graceful with beauty, all with unfallen breasts, / highly skilled in the techniques of love, and therefore entirely confident,
wearing very fine garments, with glances unsteady like lightning: / by whoever dance is arranged with such women
for even a single day, O king, he will dwell for years on an aerial chariot, / his face watched by a hundred women, youthful, worshipped by many,
full of an increase of bliss, free from anger, envy, and the like, / his limbs smeared with the five perfumes, his face [delighted] with camphor and betel nut,
resembling the sun; and the women are all endowed with such teeth, / bearing garlands made of newly blossomed, fragrant pārijāta flowers,
all possessing blossoming hips, wearing garlands joined with red [flowers], / wearing them in their braids and upon their breasts, with smiling lips.
Accompanied by such [women], he moves about, delighted by dance and song. / Having thus ascended an aerial chariot and dwelt for an imperishable time,
he will afterwards be born as a king; having acted thus again, / having enjoyed a kingdom as the fruit of heaven, he will become a devotee of Śiva.
Śambhu said: / What Vasiṣṭha told Dilīpa, Aṅgiras told to the sages. / They acted accordingly, and performed the threefold arts of dance, song, and music for the Lord of Umā.
Having listened to the complete Padma Purāṇa, they became joyful. / Those very brāhmaṇas, O Rāma, seated on an excellent celestial chariot,
are seen in the sky, joyful, their minds ever delighted. / All this has been related to you, firmly established in the Purāṇas.
Beyond this, what more do you wish to hear, O Rāghava?

5.114.m: Rāma said: / Who is this that is seen in the sky, adorned with all ornaments, / mounted on a celestial chariot, endowed with great brilliance, like a second midday sun,
hard to look upon for all mortals? In his lap is a sweetly smiling woman, / like another Śrī, O holy one, and likewise five fair maidens.
They sing a sweet song with glances from arched eyebrows, / with gentle smiles, and with the clapping of their hands;
sometimes with songs produced from the throat, with striking of one another's hands, / gazing into one another's faces, with enticements preceded by songs.
Sporting thus sits the great yogin, resembling the filaments of a lotus. / By what meritorious conduct of this kind [did he attain this]? Tell that to me!
Śambhu said: / Formerly, O Rāma, this vipra possessed all kinds of wealth, / endowed with various pleasures, dedicated to supporting his wife;
he was sonless, devoid of charity, and avoided the worship of deities; / he lacked the five great sacrifices and was devoid of Vedic recitation;
intent on eating in the morning, at noon, and in the evening; impure. / Once he went to the house of the great-souled Gautama,
on the sacred mountain of Tryambaka, resorted to by hosts of various sages. / Even there, his house was splendid, constructed with crystal pillars,
whose walls were smeared with aloe liquid, musk, camphor, and saffron, / possessing the elegance of the fragrance of santāna blossoms;
its floor sprinkled with musk and floral nectar; / adorned with fine, exceedingly white, varied canopies;
its courtyard adorned and beautified with large plantain and betel-nut trees; / nearby was a lotus pool where bees hummed charmingly;
the quarters were filled with the fragrance arising from sandalwood trees; / the quarters were filled with songs that brought delight through tutored singing;
fitted with mechanical devices that destroyed the heat caused by summer; / its roof constructed to ward off the sun, covered with plantain leaves;
having thick door-panels made of very smooth sandalwood; / its inner walls fashioned with the exceedingly delightful scent of fragrant water-lilies;
having an altar fashioned for delight, auspicious in the northeast direction; / its base constructed of gold, furnished with a variegated altar;
fashioned at the root of a banyan tree with very glossy, dense shade; / its surroundings beautified by blossoms, plantain groves, and lakes;
with clouds cooled as they touched the crest of the great banyan; / adorned with variegated pleasure-gardens endowed like celestial groves;
beautified with stepped wells, wells, ponds, and numerous woods; / where the wind blew very gently into the house, imparting comfort.
And there were female instrumentalists, lovely in all their limbs, their musical instruments a wealth of erotic charm; / excellent women played the lute, the flute, and the triveṇu flute;
the women performed the threefold arts in the four directions and above. / In vessels of gold and other [metals] were auspicious balls of sacred ash,
scented with all kinds of perfumes and fumigated with fine incense; / and there were bundles tied with kuśa grass and rosaries by the millions;
and thousands of black antelope skins were kept at the outer borders. / In such an excellent house, the lord of sages, revered by the gods,
having placed camphor and other items in the four directions, the lord of sages / fashioned a camphor lion-throne upon a sandalwood seat,
fine, white, and very smooth, surrounded with camphor. / Having bathed Śaṅkara with fragrant, scented waters and milk,
and having bathed Sadāśiva with other Vedic mantras, / placing a cloth seat upon the wooden moon-dais, / setting the worship tray in front, and placing these items upon the petals:
in one vessel unmutilated grains, in another unmutilated grains mixed with sesame; / the five fragrances in one, the eight fragrances in another;
placing saffron, musk, camphor, and sandalwood / in other vessels and arranging them at the place of worship;
the worship is performed there according to the method of multiple enclosures: / the god Sadāśiva, with five faces, resides in the middle of the liṅga;
his outer enclosure is the liṅga, and Śakti is prescribed for it; / the enclosure of Śakti is Viṣṇu, and the enclosure of Viṣṇu is Brahmā;
the enclosure of Brahmā is the Moon, and his is the Sun; then the Vedas; / their concealment is in the regents of the directions, and the enclosure of those is the directions;
the enclosure of the directions is Śambhu, and his enclosure is the qualities. / This indeed is the auspicious worship of Śiva's liṅga with ten enclosures.
Such may be the opinion of some; now the other [systems of] enclosures: / knowledge is declared as an enclosure, and that is considered the enclosure of Umā;
Viṣṇu is her surrounding enclosure, and Brahmā is the enclosure of Viṣṇu; / the moon is the enclosure of Brahmā, and the sun is its enclosure.
and the enclosure of the Sun is the Lord—thus the sixfold enclosure is remembered. / Without Brahmā, it is declared to be the excellent fivefold enclosure;
this is the triad of enclosures of the Moon, Viṣṇu, and the Śaktis. / The enclosure of Ambikā is declared to be an excellent single enclosure.
Or the world protectors may be the enclosure in the worship of the Moon-crested one; / or worship without any enclosure is praised for Śiva.
One should worship Śiva with the substances placed on the eight petals of the tray. / I will declare the characteristics of the tray, useful for all rituals:
fashioned of gold, silver, or copper, / one should make the auspicious eight-petalled tray resembling a pearl oyster shell;
one should fashion it with eight corners equal to lotus petals; / a measure of one pala is then commended, completed, its surface broad,
its middle not thick, with eight petals having the form of a lotus on top; / or, according to the path of Śakti, one may fashion it with five petals;
or one may make it with three petals, according to the view based on devotional feeling; / the wise person should make it in such a manner that the vessel is handsome.
An auspicious garland made of one hundred and eight rudrākṣa beads interspersed with śakti [beads], / and a sacred thread fashioned with thirty-eight [beads];
having tied one on each upper arm, and two on the forearms, / one was worn on the head by that supreme sage, and one on the neck;
a rosary fashioned of rudrākṣa beads, crystal, and gems. / Making a seat of tiger skin, the sage seated in the lotus posture,
having performed the invocation, offering of a seat, water for the hands, water for the feet, and water for sipping, / bathed Śaṅkara with the waters of the Gaṅgā;
with flowers blended with the eight fragrances, with bakula and pāṭala blossoms, / kept in golden vessels, purified with cloth, and thoroughly perfumed;
and at the door was an auspicious copper caldron with a continuous channel; / with a cow's horn, or sometimes with the horn of a gayal,
or with a right-whorled conch shell, or with vessels of gems, / or with golden, silver, copper, or bell-metal ones,
and with fine golden pots, he bathed [the liṅga] according to desire; / or one may perform it with earthen vessels, or with lotus leaves.
One should bathe the all-pervading Lord with vessels made of palāśa, mango, rose-apple, and other [leaves or woods]; / but of all ablutions, a continuous stream of water is praised as foremost.
With the hymn beginning with 'namaste' known as the Śatarudriya, / and with the anuvāka beginning with 'śaṃ ca' which is of the nature of peace, [one worships] the Lord.
Having repeated it according to one's ability, he should then apply perfumes and other offerings; / and after that, he should worship with lovely flowers, leaves, and bilva leaves,
with tulasī, māruva leaves, kalhāra flowers, and great water-lilies, / with blue water-lilies, lotuses, and the remaining oleander flowers,
with karṇikāras, white lotuses, and likewise aparājitā blossoms; / with sesame and unbroken rice grains, with unbroken grains alone, and with bilva leaves mixed with sesame.
In this manner Gautama worshiped the great Lord, Īśāna, / with camphor, agallochum, musk, resin, and sandalwoods.
He incensed Him with these and other substances, and then [offered] sixteen small lamps, / furnished with camphor wicks and placed upon a lamp-stand.
Then an excellent food offering was presented to the great Lord: / well-cooked rice from śāli grains, foods made of flour, foods to be chewed, licked, and sucked,
accompanied by sweet and other savors, provided with the five kinds of foods, / rich with many cooked vegetables, and mixed with various prepared dishes,
accompanied by twenty kinds of drinks, furnished with grapes and plantains, / provided with the eight kinds of broths, and equipped with roots, fruits, and the like.
Arranged also with other items according to availability, / and accompanied by the foremost flowers, the sage presented this food offering.
Having offered a thousand waving lights placed upon a golden platter / to the God along with offerings, and having bowed low,
and then scraped pieces of betel-nut, and washed leaves / free of stalks and tips, wrapped in pure white folds,
with camphor powder and an auspicious triad of laid leaves, / this betel placed on a golden plate he offered unto the Lord.
Then, having circumambulated, and after prostrations, / eight maidens then arrived, bearing lutes, flutes, and other instruments.
Playing various musical instruments, they came near the sage; / taking up a pair of small cymbals, he himself began to sing.
When Gautama began to sing, the maidens took up the melody; / and other women played the musical instruments very softly.
As the sage sang sweetly, the musical notes, taking physical form, / danced before the great Lord; that was like a wonder.
At that moment arrived the blessed sage Nārada. / Gautama also, having worshiped and bowed down to him who had arrived,
said to him: 'I am fulfilled today, and there is none equal to me. / What is the purpose of your coming, and from where do you come?'
The venerable Nārada said: / 'I have come here from Pātāla after eating in Bāṇa’s residence. / The great-souled ones, Bāṇa, Śukra, and others, will soon come to your abode.'
Then in an instant Bāṇa arrived, the conqueror of enemy cities; / accompanied by twenty akṣauhiṇīs, that asura rode upon an elephant.
Śukra [mounted] another elephant, Prahlāda an excellent chariot, / Vṛṣaparvan a splendid chariot, and Bali an excellent horse.
Having learned that all of them had arrived, Gautama, / accompanied by his disciples, went out with haste, taking water for guest-offering and the rest.
And seeing Gautama, they dismounted from their elephants and other mounts; / having bowed to that descendant of Bhṛgu, the daityas then made obeisance [to Gautama].
Having embraced all the rākṣasas and honored them according to the rules, / the eminent sage arranged an encampment for the army.
Having washed the feet of Śukra, the water was placed upon his head; / and the sage gave a guest-offering endowed with various fruits.
Having performed their rites preceded by bathing in wells, ponds, and lakes, / at the confluence in Gautama's auspicious hermitage,
the rākṣasas together with their priest entered his house, / and all performed worship of God and self-surrender in the dwelling of the twice-born.
On an altar quickly prepared, Śukra worshiped Śiva; / on his left side, Prahrāda worshiped Acyuta;
Bali likewise worshiped Soma, and other chiefs among the asuras [worshiped their deities]; / then Bāṇa worshiped the one God, the three-eyed Lord alone.
Śukra also worshiped the blessed Lord, the husband of Umā; / and Gautama then worshiped Śaṅkara at midday.
All wore white garments, their bodies smeared with ashes; / with white ash they had made the triple-mark across every place [on their bodies].
Having bowed to the descendant of Bhṛgu, all began the purification of elements: / within the hollow in the center of the heart-lotus are the five elements;
in their midst is the great space, and in that space is the immaculate fire; / in the midst of that one should meditate on the great Lord, full of light and auspicious.
One should burn with the fire of knowledge that body, / an elemental form connected with ignorance, contaminated, joined to all [defilements], within the lamp of space.
Having burned the 'I' that envelops space, he should then burn space; / having burned the wind consisting of space, he should then burn the fire element.
And then, having burned the water element and the earth element, / and having burned the qualities dependent on them, he should thereafter burn the body.
Having thus burned the elements by that fire of knowledge, the embodied soul [should contemplate] / Viṣṇu situated in the center of the flame, brimming with the essence of bliss,
Śiva, whose rays resemble the radiance of the perfected moon; / with the rays born from the limbs of Śiva, united with the nectar-fluid,
the flame, exceedingly cool, became completely calmed like moonbeams; / and the flood became dense with the shed rays of nectar.
One should contemplate the supreme [Lord] as having gradually inundated the aggregate of elements.

Having thus performed the purification of elements, a mortal becomes fit for rites and truly pure; / in performing worship and the recitation of mantras, and thereafter in meditating on God, the destruction of [sins such as] the slaying of a brahmin occurs.

Having thus meditated on Him who has the radiance of moonlight, having swiftly placed Him into Śiva's linga by meditation, / and having contemplated Sadāśiva in the center of the lamp, the worship is performed with the imperishable five-syllable mantra.
Having performed the invocations and other services, and the bath of Śaṅkara as before, / [one should prepare] a copper, silver, or gold seat, or any seat here covered with cloth and the like.

Having finally made a shower of water-bubbles upon each pedestal, / one should place one serpent in front on the pedestal, and a pair of serpents above on the pedestal, to the right and left near the God.

Having placed a hibiscus flower between the serpents, and in the center a cloth folded twelve times, / in its center the great Lord, endowed with the form of a linga and pedestal, is to be worshiped with pure white [offerings].

Having done this, Bāṇa and the other chiefs of the sons of Diti, repeatedly offering the five scents and eight scents, / and having worshiped with flowers, leaves, bilva leaves, sesame, unbroken rice, mixed with sesame, and plain [rice],

having offered incense duly applied, having offered a lamp and the very food offerings prescribed, / all of them, having completed the remainder of the worship, performed song and dance in various places.
Now at that moment, Gautama's disciple named Śaṅkarātman arrived.
He had the appearance of a madman, naked, adopting various disguises; / in one place he seemed the best of brahmins, in another like a Caṇḍāla,
in one place like a Śūdra, a yogin, and in another even an ascetic; / he roared and leaped, danced, praised, and sang;
he wept, listened clearly, fell down, and rose up somewhere; / endowed solely with the knowledge of Śiva, he was filled with supreme bliss.
Arriving at mealtime, he went near Gautama; / he ate together with his guru, and sometimes [ate] his leftovers.
Sometimes he licked the dish; sometimes he went away in silence; / sometimes he grasped his guru's hand and ate himself.
Sometimes he urinated inside the house; sometimes he smeared it with mud. / Always seeing him thus, the guru took him by the hand to the house,
brought him in, seated him on his own seat, and fed him; / the sage Gautama himself ate from his dish.
Then once, in order to test his mind, the beautiful, / auspicious Ahalyā summoned the disciple and said, "Eat!"
Having placed food in a golden dish, and in another cup / having offered drink and other [refreshments], she then placed fire in one [vessel],
having placed a heap of burning coals, and in another a heap of thorns, / [saying,] "Eat, eat!" And the sage ate it.
Just as the twice-born drank the water, so he also consumed the fire; / having eaten even the thorns, he remained as before.
Indeed, long ago, invited by the daughters of the sages to eat, / he was given day after day a clod of earth, water, and cow dung,
mud, and a wooden staff; having eaten them with joy, he was delighted. / Such was this sage, resembling an outcaste in appearance.
Holding very worn-out sandals in his hand, / he approached Vṛṣaparvan, speaking words suited to an outcaste.
Clad only in the quarters of the sky, he stood between Vṛṣaparvan and the lord. / Not recognizing him, Vṛṣaparvan tormented him and severed his head.
When that best of the twice-born was slain, this world of moving and unmoving beings / became exceedingly corrupted, as did the sages who resided there.
A great grief arose in Gautama, the very great-souled one; / water flowed from his eyes as if displaying his sorrow.
In the presence of all the Daityas, Gautama spoke these words: / "What sin was committed by him that his head has been severed?
He was dearer to me than life, a yogin devoted always to Śiva. / Truly, my own death will follow, for the guru is embodied in the disciple.
Where death is seen to befall Śaivas who are devoted to dharma / and who always follow Śiva's path, there our death is certain!"
Śukra said: / "I shall revive him, who belongs to my lineage and is beloved of Śiva! / Why should he die, O brāhmaṇa? Behold the power of my asceticism!"
While the foremost among brāhmaṇas was speaking thus, Gautama died; / and when he died, Śukra also abandoned his vital breaths through yoga.
Knowing that he too was killed, the lords of the Dānavas led by Prahlāda / all died in that very instant; it was marvelous indeed.
Then the army of the wise Bāṇa also died. / Burning with grief, Ahalyā wept aloud again and again.
The all-pervading lord who was worshipped through Gautama's worship of Maheśa, / Vīrabhadra, the great yogin, seeing everything, became enraged:
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! Many devotees of Maheśvara have died! / I shall inform Śiva; I shall do whatever he tells me."
Having decided thus, he went to the imperishable Mount Mandara; / having bowed to Virūpākṣa, he then related all this to him.
Seeing Brahmā and Hari standing there, Śiva spoke these words; / seeing the daring deed done by my devotees, he who grants boons [said]:
"Let us go and see, O Viṣṇu! You two shall come as well." / Then the Lord mounted the bull, fanned by the chowrie in the wind,
with Nandika handsomely attired holding the exceedingly beautiful umbrella / with a bright white golden staff, held over the Lord with unrivaled fitness.
Having obtained Maheśa's permission, Hari stood near his serpent, / resplendent with the Kaustubha gem visible under reddish and dark-blue parasols.
With Śiva's permission, Brahmā too mounted his swan; / the Ordainer shone beneath parasols possessing the luster of cochineal insects.
All the gods beginning with Indra, accompanied by their respective mounts, / then departed together, delighted by various musical instruments.
Surrounded by tens of millions of gaṇas, they went to Gautama's hermitage. / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, having seen that supreme wonder,
revived his devotee simply by looking from the corner of his left eye. / Śaṅkara said to Gautama: "I am pleased with you; choose a boon!"
Gautama said: / "If you are pleased, O Lord of the gods, if a boon is to be given to me, / let me have the continuous capacity to worship your linga, O Maheśvara!
This boon has been chosen by me, O God! Listen to this, O three-eyed one: / my disciple is highly fortunate, free from [notions of] what is to be discarded and what is not,
he does not look with his eyes upon what should be viewed as 'mine', / nor should anything be smelled with his nose, nor given, nor anything else;
Understanding this and acting accordingly, that renowned yogin, / appearing mad and deformed, was celebrated as the self of Śaṅkara.
Let no one hate him, and let no one harm him! / Let this be given to me, O God, and likewise freedom from death for these [others]."
The Blessed Lord said: / "Let these live until the end of the kalpa, and then let them attain liberation. / This spacious, variegated, and auspicious dwelling was prepared by you;
we shall stay here for just a moment, and then we will go home." / Gautama said: "I am requesting what is unfitting, O Lord, for one who desires does not see faults.
Give that which is unobtainable even by Brahmā and others, O Lord of the gods, if it pleases you." / Then the Lord looked at Viṣṇu, and taking Hari's hand,
laughing, Sadāśiva spoke thus to the lotus-eyed one: / "Your belly is shriveled, O Govinda! Shall food be given to you?
Either enter yourself and eat by yourself, as in your own home, / or go to Pārvatī's house, she who will fill your belly."
Having said this, holding his hand, the all-powerful Lord went to solitude, / having instructed Nandin, the guardian of the door, as prescribed.
He spoke this reply to Gautama regarding Viṣṇu's words: / Sadāśiva said: "Procure food for everyone; we wish to eat, O sage!"
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara went to a solitary place with Vāsudeva; / ascending a soft couch, the two supreme deities lay down.
Having conversed with each other, both arose; / going to a deep pool, the two best of gods prepared to bathe.
Cupfuls of water were drunk from the hands by each party separately; / the sages and the rākṣasas engaged in water-sports.
Then Viṣṇu and Maheśa quickly splashed water [at each other]; / with cupped hands filled with lotus filaments, Śaṅkara
scattered them over Hari's face, whose eyes were wide like bloomed lotuses. / Keśava closed his eyes due to the fall of the filaments.
Meanwhile, Maheśvara climbed onto Hari's shoulders; / taking hold of Hari's head with both arms, he plunged him down.
Bringing him up again, and again and again, / being thus afflicted, Hari subtly threw Śaṅkara down.
Then, seizing both his feet, he dragged him and whirled him around; / he struck Hari's chest and threw Acyuta down.
Then Hari, having stood up, took water in his cupped hands and / splashed it over Śambhu, and Hara then splashed it over Viṣṇu.
Such was the water-sport; and among the assembly of ṛṣis, / their braided hair came undone in the excitement of the water-sport.
Then, in their confusion, the knots of their matted locks became entangled with one another; / their matted locks being bound to each other, the lords of sages [laughed].
The strong pulled the weak, causing them pain, / dragging them down elsewhere as they cried out and wept.
When this tumultuous water-play was underway, / Nārada in the sky, delighted, danced and shouted aloud.
Sounding the viṇā instrument, he sang a graceful song; / with that sweet, graceful song he sang in ten variations.
Śaṃkara, who brings forth the worlds, heard the sweet song, / and he himself slowly began to sing gracefully.
As the Lord of Gods himself was singing the mixed Maṅgalakaiśikī mode, / and Nārada was dancing and singing with varied notes,
taking up the steady pitch endowed with every proper quality, / [Hanumān] then surpassed them with his singing, full of the nectar of its own flow.
Vāsudeva beat this mardala drum with both hands; / diving into the tune, the four-faced [Brahmā] and Tuṃburu resonated with loud voices.
Gautama and the others who were singers fell silent from singing at once, / when Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, sang a sweet song.
What was withered became un-withered; the emaciated became nourished then; / abandoning their respective songs, everyone was thus enraptured.
All the celestial sages and Dānavas fell silent; / Hanumān alone was the singer, and they were all listeners.
When noon had fully arrived, it being the time for eating, / Maheśvara put on a pair of fine silk garments while listening to the song.
Viṣṇu [put on] two yellow garments, and the four-faced [Brahmā] reddish ones; / and all of them put on garments fitting for themselves after performing their midday duties.
All the deities departed, mounting their respective vehicles; / and Maheśa, who loves singing, addressed the lord of monkeys:
“O monkey, commanded by me, mount the bull without fear; / facing me, sing every song!”
Then the tiger among monkeys said to the blessed Maheśvara: / “The capacity to mount the bull belongs to you, not to anyone else.
If I mount your vehicle, O omnipresent one, I would become a sinner; / mount me instead, O Lord of Gods, [as your] bird, Śiva's mount!
And behold, I will sing facing you!” / Then the Lord mounted Hanumān just like a bull.
When Lord Śaṃkara had mounted, Hanumān, twisting the skin / of his neck and head around, sang facing him as before.
Listening to the nectar of the song, Śambhu went to Gautama’s house, / and all the celestial sages and Dānavas came there as well.
They were then honoured by Gautama at the mealtime; / whatever household utensils and the like were made of dry wood,
all sprouted into life while Hanumān was singing! / The astonished gaze of everyone remained fixed upon that singing.
Two-armed, saluting the feet of the Lord, adorned with all ornaments, / cheerful in form, youthful, [Hanumān] stood in their midst with his head bowed, praised by the gods with joined palms.
Holding his head with both hands, Śaṃkara turned Hanumān’s face toward the east; / Hanumān being seated in the lotus posture, [Śiva] placed one foot in his folded palms and the other in his mouth.

Then with his toes the omnipresent Lord very gently touched [Hanumān’s] nose with affection; / on the shoulder, on the face, on the collarbone, on the throat, on the chest, on the heart between the breasts,
and then on the belly, then on the navel region, and then placed his second foot into the folded palms; / grasping his head and bending it down, Śaṃkara audibly touched his back with his chin.
And Śiva placed a necklace fashioned of pearls upon Hanumān’s neck. / Then Viṣṇu spoke these words to Maheśāna:
“There is none equal to Hanumān in the entire circle of the universe; / for your abode, inaccessible even to the Vedas and gods, is established [in him].
Your abode, unmanifest in all the Upaniṣads, is fully possessed by this monkey; / your foot did not dwell for even a moment through yogas with restraints and other means,
nor in the lotus-heart of the great yogis, but its pure power rests in Hanumān! / Even after performing difficult austerities for thousands of millions of years,
the lords of sages do not know your form, let alone your foot! / Oh, wondrous is the fortune of this fickle wild monkey,
that he holds both your feet on his body, a grace not granted even to the hearts of yogis! / Though I worshipped you with devotion daily for a thousand years,
and for another thousand years, O Lord, your foot was not shown by you. / There is a great saying in the world: ‘Śambhu is dear to Nārāyaṇa,
and Hari is dear to Śambhu’—yet I do not possess such fortune!” / Sadāśiva said: “No one is as dear to me as you, O blessed Hari;
only Pārvatī is equal to you, and no other exists for me.” / Then Gautama, bowing down before that great god,
entreated: “O boundless-souled one, O god, come, O treasure of compassion! / Midday has passed, and it is the mealtime for all.”
Then the omnipresent Mahādeva, having sipped water along with Viṣṇu, / entered Gautama’s house and sat down to eat.

With jewelled rings and anklets, with a fastening of fine cloth, with an exquisite belt like lightning, / with many necklaces, and then a neck-ornament of coins, a sacred thread, and an upper garment;
with dangling, glittering jewel earrings, with his excellent braided hair adorned with flowers, the god [shone], / with an unguent of fivefold perfumes, with armlets, bracelets, and rings.

Thus adorned, Śiva sat upon an excellent seat, and likewise seated Hari facing him on an excellent seat. / As Hari and the Lord stood facing one another, Gautama, best of the gods, then presented golden vessels.

The sage provided thirty kinds of edible food, four kinds of excellent milk-rice, two hundred well-cooked preparations, / three hundred mixed dishes of uncooked and cooked foods, a hundred kinds of good roots, and likewise a hundred kinds of vegetables,

and he gave twenty-five vegetables and the like mixed with clarified butter, fine sugar and so forth, lime, pomegranate, and the like, / plantains, grapes, good dates, oranges, rose apples, priyāla fruits, and vikaṅkata fruits.
Having offered these and other provisions according to rule, / and having given the water for sipping before eating, the brāhmaṇa said, “Please eat!”
And while they all were eating, Gautama himself / took up a fan made of fine cloth and fanned Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Then the Supreme Lord wished to make a joke: / “Look, Viṣṇu, at Hanūmat! How does that monkey eat?”
While Hari was looking at the monkey, Maheśvara threw / a cake into Viṣṇu’s vessel, even while the host of sages was watching.
And he gave his own leftovers of milk-rice and the rest to Hanūmat. / [The monkey said:] “Your leftover food is indeed unfit to be eaten, according to your own word, O Lord!
‘The offering made to me—leaves, flowers, and fruits—is unfit [for others]. / Having offered everything to me, one should cast it solely into a well.’
If it is uneaten, your word is indeed [kept]; yet if it is eaten, it is also your grace.” / Sadāśiva said: “When it is a Bāṇaliṅga, a self-manifested [liṅga], or one established in moonstone,
eating the offering of Śambhu is to be known as equal to a cāndrāyaṇa penance. / This is now the time for eating; it would lose its relish from another discourse.
After eating, I will tell [you]; eat that without hesitation.” / Then that sage Gautama performed the purification of the water.

He filled the water-pitchers, which were reddish, very smooth, with very fine bodies, washed in many ways, with their bodies well dried, / and purified by scrubbing with seeds using tank-water.

Having covered a brand-new sandy altar of the river with pure, exceedingly white, fine garments, he placed the jars filled with water on top.
Having thrown into it a bundle of lotus flowers and nutmeg, kakkola berries, musk powder, and sandalwood, he threw in a garland as white as moonbeams inside the bundle.
Again, after a watch of the day, having filtered the water with a cloth, he poured it into the pitcher, and placing a camphor-knot, bakula flowers, and likewise pāṭalā blossoms,

and then a cluster of night-flowering jasmine, and putting the water there, having performed the purification of the water at the very beginning, / he then wrapped the mouth of the spout and the fine rim with a piece of exceedingly soft, fine cloth.
Then, placing the pitchers in a shade free from heat, / where there was a gentle breeze and it was fanned with a fine fan,
then, O king, having purified it with subterranean waters, he sprinkled even the spout; having prepared themselves, men and women there,
or his daughters, their limbs bathed, wearing clean garments, / with honey-yellow resin and thick liquid agallochum,
smearing it thickly on the armpits and on the neck, / placing a prayer-amulet on the head, with an unguent of five perfumes,
their fair hair bound with flowers, having auspicious faces, thoroughly spotless— / in this very manner suitable women, their bodies adorned with saffron,
young women with lovely limbs and adorned with ornaments, / through such women or men he had the water served.
At the time of offering, having placed a small wrapper of fine cloth, / or the pitcher in the left hand, look there!
Releasing what was fastened with a cord, he then had the water given. / In this manner, the venerable sage Gautama showed hospitality.
When Maheśa and all the great-souled ones had eaten, / with their feet and hands washed and their hands rubbed with fragrant paste,
while the great lord, god of gods, was seated on that seat, / and then the gods with the hosts of sages were seated lower down,
having enclosed in jewelled vessels pieces of betel-nut well fumigated with incense, / not angular, round, thick, neither too small nor too thin,
and having cleaned white betel leaves, adding pieces of camphor / and lime, as Gautama was offering it to Śaṅkara,
when the sage spoke the words, “O God, take the betel,” / [Śiva said:] “O monkey, take the betel and give me the pieces!”
The monkey said: “O Maheśvara, I have no purity. / Because of having eaten many fruits, how can a monkey be pure?”
Sadāśiva said: “By my word everything is purified; by my word poison becomes nectar. / By my word all the Vedas exist; by my word the deities and the rest exist.
By my word comes the knowledge of dharma; by my word liberation is proclaimed. / The Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Smṛtis exist solely through my word.
Therefore, take the betel and give me the fine pieces.” / Hari took the betel and the pieces of betel-nut with his left hand.
Then, taking the leaves, he presented the pieces; / having taken the camphor offered before him, Śiva ate it.
While the god was chewing betel, Pārvatī came from Mount Mandara / to the sage’s house, taking the hands of Jayā and Vijayā.
Having bowed to the god’s feet, she stood with downcast face. / Lifting up her face, the three-eyed Lord said this:
“On your account, O goddess of the lord of gods, I have committed an offense, / in that I ate without you; hear another thing, O beautiful one!
Having left you in my own abode, destitute of the god of gods, / and abandoned by all relatives, a great sin was committed by me.
You should forgive me, O goddess of gods! Cast away your anger and look [at me]!” / Addressed thus, she did not speak, but went out with Arundhatī.
Knowing that she was leaving, the sage bowed down like a staff. / From that time on, one should perform prostrations like a staff and praises to the great lord.
And Śivā said: “Gautama, what do you desire?” / Gautama said: “I have accomplished my purpose, O goddess of gods, if a boon is to be given to me:
You should eat now in my house, O highly fortunate one!” / The goddess said: “I will eat in your house, O sage, with Śaṅkara's consent.”
Having gone to the Lord, the brāhmaṇa Gautama, having obtained permission, returned; / he fed the Mountain’s daughter and Arundhatī.
Having eaten everything, Pārvatī, adorned with perfumes and flowers, / went to Hara together with thousands of attendant maidens.
Then Śaṅkara said to the goddess: “Go to Gautama’s house. / Having performed the twilight worship, I will come home again.”
Addressed thus, the goddess went to the house of Gautama; / and desiring to perform the twilight prayers, everyone went outside.
Having performed the twilight prayers at the pond, Maheśa and all the others, / Śambhu, facing north and having performed the ritual nyāsa, muttered his prayers.
Then Viṣṇu of great splendour said this to Maheśa: / “You who are bowed to by all, who are worshipped by all,
to whom offerings are made in all sacrifices—what will your noble self murmur? / All stand with folded hands and worship only you alone;
to whom do you yourself, O Lord of the gods of gods, fold your hands? / You, O Maheśvara, are the giver of the fruit of merits such as obeisances;
who is your rewarder, who is to be revered by you, or who is higher than you? Tell me.” / Śaṃkara said: “I do not meditate on anything, O Govinda; I bow to nothing;
I worship nothing, O Hari; I murmur nothing. / But in order to guide atheistic beings onto the path,
this must be shown by me, O Hari; otherwise they would become evildoers. / Therefore, for the benefit of the world, all this has been done by me.”
Saying ‘Om’, Hari then bowed to him and stood by. / Then the celestial sages reached Gautama’s house;
they all performed worship to the god of gods who holds the Pināka bow. / The Lord remained singing along with Hanumān, O best of the Raghus.
All of them then muttered the five-syllable great spell. / Holding Hanumān’s hand, Hara went near the goddess.
Both of the divine couple sat on a single couch; / Hanumān, Tuṃburu, and Nārada sat there singing.
The Supreme Lord indulged in various sports; / summoning Pārvatī, the Lord spoke these words:
The venerable Sadāśiva said: “I shall arrange your braided hair; come before me, O fair one!” / The goddess said: “It is not proper for a husband to attend upon his wife.
In dressing my hair, a grave disaster might occur; / in the dressing of hair, O Lord, everything is not as desired.
And when the braid is tied, then comes wiping the edges of the shoulders, / wiping off the hairs, flowers, and other things adhering to the back of the body.
While this is going on, if the great souls should arrive, / what answer can then be given, O Lord, to those who praise you, the gods and others?
If they do not come, O Lord, then fear will vanish.” / As she was speaking thus, Śaṃkara pulled her by the hand,
seated her on his own thighs, untied the knot of her hair, / divided it with his hands, and combed through it with his nails.
Taking the garland of pārijāta flowers given by Viṣṇu that was in her hair, / he arranged her braided hair, and then held the garland in his hand.
Taking a garland of jasmine flowers, the Great Lord tied it in the hair-knot, / and also a garland of wishing-tree blossoms given by Brahmā.
He arranged it, hidden and rich with fragrance, in Pārvatī's garment; / then the all-pervading Lord smoothed her shoulder and back.
Having reached below the loose knot of her garment, down the folds of the goddess's cloth, / the god said, "What is this?" and tied the garment-knot.
"I see this nose-ornament of yours," he then passionately said; / having spoken thus, the virtuous woman herself took the lustreless pearl.
"From contact with turmeric, the pearl lacks brilliance; / let this pearl indeed be worn, which is dear to me and to you."
Pārvatī said: / "Oh Śambhu, your house is indeed abundant in all things! / Earlier, I knew everything merely by your ornaments.
Ah, the wealth of your property is understood by your ornaments! / Your head is decorated, O god, with a garland of Brahmā's heads;
likewise, a garland of human skulls is the ornament of your chest; / and Śeṣa and Vāsuki, both venomous, are your bracelets;
the directions are your garment, matted locks your hair, and ashes your body-cosmetic; / your mount is a great bull, and your lineage and family are entirely unknown;
your parents are not known at all, and your body has odd eyes!" / As the daughter of the mountain spoke thus, Viṣṇu, highly enraged, said:
"Why do you insult the god of gods, the lord of the universe, O goddess? / I shall surely abandon my dear life-breaths, O blessed one, [because of] your lack of restraint.
Where there is insult to the Lord, O blessed one, there my vow is death!" / Having said this, Hari proceeded to sever his own head with his nails.
The Great Lord, however, grasped his hand and said: "Do not act rashly! / Every word of Pārvatī is dear to me, [though] displeasing to you.
Whatever is desired to be done that is displeasing to me, O Hṛṣīkeśa, [refrain from it]!" / Having said "Om," the blessed lord Hari then became silent.
Hanumān then addressed these words to the god: / "I request [instruction in] the desireless observance of worship for myself.
I too would go to perform worship; you ought to permit me." / Śaṅkara said: "Whose worship, where is the worship, what flower, what leaf? Tell me!
Who is the guru, what is your mantra, and what is your manner of worship?" / When the lord of gods spoke thus, Hanūmān trembled exceedingly.
With all his limbs shaking, he began to praise: / Hanūmān said: "Homage to the god, the great Śaṅkara of boundless soul!
Homage to the yogin, the upholder of yoga, and the guru of yogins! / Homage to the god reachable by yogins, to the master of the wise!
Homage to you, the lord of the Vedas, the lord of the gods! / Homage to contemplation, to him who is reachable by contemplation, the guru of creators!
Homage to the disciplined, reachable by the disciplined, the lord of the earth and the rest! / Homage to the treasure of Vedic utterances, beginning with 'namas te'!
Homage to you who are expounded by statements such as 'ātanuṣva'! / Homage to you of eight forms, homage to the lord of cattle!
To Tryambaka, to the three-eyed one, whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire; / to you who love the good bhṛṅgarāja, dhattūra, and droṇa blossoms;
and to you who love bṛhatī, areca, puṃnāga, campaka, and others; / homage to you, homage to you, again and again homage, homage!"
Śiva then said to Hari: "Do not fear; tell me everything." / Hanumān said: "Worship of the Śivaliṅga should be performed by one whose body is dusted with ashes,
with waters procured by day, and likewise with flowers and the like. / O god, I shall describe the auspicious rule for the worship of Śiva.
When evening time has arrived, one should perform a bath without [wetting] the head; / putting on a washed, dry garment, the person of keen intellect should sip water twice.
Then, taking ashes, one should perform the fiery bath, / having consecrated it with the praṇava, either eight times or else
with the five-syllable mantra or with any [divine] name whatsoever. / Holding darbha grass in hand, one should take the ashes consecrated seven times.
Saying 'īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām', he should drop [ashes] on the head; / saying 'tatpuruṣāya vidmahe', he should sprinkle ashes on the face;
saying 'aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyaḥ', he should cast ashes on the chest; / saying 'vāmadevāya namaḥ', he should apply it to the private parts;
saying 'sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi', he should apply it to the feet; / with the praṇava, the discerning person should dust all his limbs.
The excellent procedure of bathing and the rest has been proclaimed for members of the three twice-born classes; / I shall declare that for Śūdras and others, as stated by the guru:
The wise person, uttering the word 'Śiva', should consecrate the ashes; / then, taking it seven times, saying 'śivāya', he should cast it on the head;
saying 'śaṅkarāya' on the face, saying 'sarvajñāya' he should cast it on the heart; / saying 'sthāṇave namaḥ' on the private parts, and saying 'svayambhuve'

having uttered it, and cast the pure ashes on both feet, / then uttering 'namaḥ śivāya', the dusting of all limbs is traditionally prescribed.

Having washed both hands and sipped water, holding darbha grass in hand with a concentrated mind— / in the absence of darbha grass there may be gold, in its absence the hair of a cow;
in its absence there may be dūrvā grass, and in its absence silver. / Having performed the twilight worship and recitation of the goddess, he should go to the house of the god,
either to an altar of the god or to an arranged bare ground, / or an arranged, clean [ground] made of clay, provided with designs of lotuses and the like,
with powders of four colors, or again with white alone, / [fashioning] diverse lotuses, and likewise the svastika and the like,
blue lotuses and the like, a mace, a conch, a trident, a ḍamaru drum, / an earthen five-chambered palace, and also a Śivaliṅga,
a wish-fulfilling tree, a kulaka, a kolaka, / a hexagon, a triangle, or a nonagon,
a twelve-cornered swing, sandals, fans, / a pair of chowries and parasols, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the like;
the wise person should draw [these] with powders on the altar or in the temple; / wherever worship of the god takes place, there the wise person should arrange it thus.
What is fashioned by one's own hand is best, what is bought is mediocre, / what is begged is inferior, and what is obtained by force is lowest.
What is [obtained by force] among worthy people, or indeed among unworthy people, by force is fruitless. / With red rice, japā flowers, and grains of white and red kalama,
with husked grains derived from wild rice, and with ears [of grain] in due order, / described as best, mediocre, and inferior,
by establishing lotuses and the like, he should perform that sacrifice properly, / facing northeast, or he should face east.
I shall also declare the seat as seen and as heard [in scripture]: / made of kuśa grass, skin, equal to cloth, wooden, palm-leaf,
woolen, golden, silver, or copper, / or one may arrange a seat made of dried cow dung or arka leaves.
Tiger skin, ruru-deer skin, deer skin, and blackbuck skin— / skin is to be known as fourfold; or of bandhuka cloth.
One should arrange a seat from among these according to availability, / having adopted the lotus posture or the auspicious posture;
seated on darbha grass and ashes, restraining the breath and keeping silent, / having assumed the form of the deity for that long, one should perform contemplation internally:
upon Śiva of subtle body, stationed twelve finger-breadths beyond the crown of the head, / moving within living beings, in the heart-cave, embodied in all forms,
endowed with all ornaments, possessing the qualities of the power of miniaturization and the rest; / having contemplated him, one should hold him in the mind, and fill the body with his pervasion.
By that radiance, the sin residing in the body is destroyed, / just as red gold becomes white through contact with quicksilver.
Having arranged a pure seat surrounded by twelve petals, / or eight, five, or three, and placing the liṅga there,
he should then meditate upon the Great Lord residing in the cave as within the liṅga. / In a purified pitcher, having cast purified, perfumed water,
and fragrant flowers, consecrated with the Praṇava— / breath-control and the Praṇava are not prescribed for Śūdras;
in place of breath-control there is meditation, and reciting 'Śiva' in place of the syllable Oṃ— / and placing nearby the articles of worship, such as scents, flowers, and unbroken grains,
he shall then make the formal resolve: / 'I shall perform Śiva’s worship, solely for the gratification of Śiva.'
Having thus formed the intention, then performing the invocation and the rest / up to the bath, one should then arrange the bath.
With the mantra beginning with 'Namaste' according to the rite of the Śatarudrīya, / the continuous stream [of water] is known as the 'stream of liberation.'
Whoever bathes [the liṅga] with it for a month, whispering the Rudra hymns in a low voice, / once, or three times, or five, seven, or nine times,
or eleven times, or endowed with eleven repetitions— / this should be known as the 'bath of liberation,' conferring liberation within a month.
The bath may be performed with the Śaiva mantra or solely with the Praṇava, / with earthen pots, pieces of coconut, or waves [of water],
with bell-metal vessels, conches, or lotus filaments; / he should bathe the God of gods with whatever is available, as declared.
And I will declare the rule for the horn, so that it becomes fit for bathing [the liṅga]: / first having cleansed it within, he should cleanse it outside and inside;
having made it very smooth and light, he should on no account cut the tip. / Placed at the lower part with an opening channel for well-rounded streams,
endowed with kuśa grass, he should arrange the bath for the god. / In this way, the water form [of pouring] from a wild ox's horn is now described.
At the opening half of the forbidden metal, joined with an aperture at the joint, / he should shape a snake-rod curved by artifice, resembling a serpent;
at the place of the tip, a cup with an opening equal to the rod. / There indeed he should let fall the water situated in the raised mechanical pot;
or he may pour it with the other hand, or with the left hand alone. / By that, the 'stream of liberation' is made, purifying and destructive of sins.
Having thus established the God of gods, and likewise [bathing him] with the five bovine products, / he should then be bathed with the five nectars, and with the sweet triad;
having adorned the god with ornaments, the Great Lord is to be bathed again. / Then, having offered cooling services, followed by sipping water and the rest,
cloth, sacred thread, and five fragrant substances— / camphor, marjoram, or sandalwood—
or a mixture of both, he should worship the Śiva-liṅga; / or the entire pedestal filled with fragrance, according to the extent of his wealth.
Silently he should offer the services, or offer the black lotus flower; / bilva leaf, sweet marjoram, and whatever is pleasing, offering all to the best of his ability.
Incense of various substances, or bdellium alone, / combined with ghee from a brown cow, is commended above all incenses.
Having offered incense according to his capacity, and lamps of brown cow's ghee, / or offering lamps with ghee alone, and offering the food gift,
obtained according to his means, accompanied by flowers, / then giving the mouth-cleanser, and offering betel with reverence,
and circumambulation and obeisance—the worship indeed concludes thus. / Next are the five constituents of song; I will explain them to you:
singing, instrumental music, recitation of Purāṇa, dance, and humorous speech; / the waving of lamps, the folded hands of flowers, the offering of everything,
asking forgiveness, and the formal dismissal—these are declared as services. / Ornaments, an umbrella, a chowrie, a fan,
the Śaiva sacred thread, and attendance: these are the six services to the Lord. / Whoever worships Śiva with these thirty-two services,
within a single day brings about the destruction of all sins, for certain. / Worship performed with thirty-two services is indeed the highest of the high.
Sadāśiva said: / 'So it is, O best of monkeys! I declare to you your worship: / worship my pair of feet, and become the performer of all worship;
worshiping thus, worship me as in the liṅga.' / Hanumān said: 'By my guru, only the worship of the liṅga was fixed for me;
I shall perform that first, O Lord, and afterwards worship your feet.' / Having spoken thus, bowing to the Lord, he set about the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
Then, having gone to the lake shore and made a sandy altar, / he prepared a seat fashioned from palm leaves.
Having washed his feet and hands, and sipped water attentively, / he then performed the ash-bath, sipped water again, and restrained his speech.
Then, on the divine altar, he fashioned very charming lotuses; / thereafter the monkey, seated in the lotus posture on the palm-leaf [mat],
restrained his breaths with renunciation, endowed with luminous meditation, / bowed to the guru and to the Lord, and remained seated, chanting beyond this.
Then he undertook the effort to perform the worship of the god: / pure water brought in two folded leaves of palāśa;
placing the fire, consecrated three times with mantras, held in the ascetic's water-pot on his head; / having performed the invocation and other rites down to the bath;
then, taking the god into his cupped hands to bathe him, / and looking at the god, the monkey did not see the pedestal.
Seeing only the liṅga in his hands, seized with fear, / the great yogin spoke this: 'What sin have I committed,
that this Śiva-liṅga remains in my hands destitute of a pedestal? / My death today is certain if the pedestal does not arrive!
Now I shall chant the Rudra hymn; then the Great Lord will come.' / Having thus resolved in his mind, he chanted the Śatarudrīya.
Even so, the Great Lord did not arrive. Then the lord of monkeys / cast the Rudra [form/liṅga] to the ground; then Vīrabhadra arrived:
