'For what reason do you weep, O devotee? Tell me the cause of your weeping!' / Hanumān said: 'Look at this liṅga devoid of a pedestal, and at the heap of my sins!'
Vīrabhadra said: / 'If your pedestal does not come to the liṅga, do not commit a rash act! / I shall burn the world if the pedestal does not arrive!
Look, show me the liṅga, whether the pedestal has come or not!' / Then, seeing the liṅga and that the pedestal had not come,
desiring to burn all the worlds, the powerful Vīrabhadra / hurled fire upon the earth; then, in an instant, the earth was burned.
Then, having burned the seven subterranean realms, it proceeded upwards again: / it burned five upper worlds, along with the inhabitants of Janaloka.
Taking with his nail the fire born from the eye on his forehead, / and making it resemble a jambīra fruit in the palm of his hand, the lord [spoke]:
'If your pedestal does not arrive, the worlds will be burned, without a doubt!' / Then, seeing that it had not arrived, the powerful Vīrabhadra—
Sanaka and the other great souls, knowing [this] through yoga, arrived, / and coming to the excellent hermitage of Gautama, the Great Lord—
the twice-born did not see the Primeval God, even though he was present; / then they praised him with hymns originating from all the Vedas:
'Obeisance to the God of gods, to him whose form is pure radiance, beyond thought! / Obeisance to the sovereign of the gods, to him who is hidden in the Vedas, the Pure One!'

Homage to Śiva, the primeval deity; homage to him whose sacred thread is a serpent; / homage to him who showers abundance of divine bliss, the sustainer of the universe in a drop of the triad of Vedas!
Earth, wind, space, water, and also moon, fire, sun, and self— / he whose eight forms are these, to that Śaṅkara, forever knowable through wisdom, homage!
Then, having heard this hymn of praise, Śiva, who restores Bhaga's eyes, / said to Viṣṇu: “Go and bring those twice-born ones here.”
Brought by Hari, they bowed low before the god. / Śaṅkara spoke these words to them: “For what reason have you come?”
The sages said: / “O Lord, piles of ashes of the twelve worlds are seen. / This single forest alone remains standing; behold the destruction of the world!”
Sadāśiva said: / “We have doubt regarding the burning of the five upper worlds. / How was there a shower of burning embers, and how was there not a great roar?”
The sages said: / “Right now our fear comes from Vīrabhadra; / it was he who drank that shower of embers as though thirsty.”
Then the god Bhava called Vīra and said, “What [is this], Vīra?” / “O hero, this was done because there was no base for Hanumat's linga;
this immense thing was done by me to test the monkey's mind.” / Then the god, an ocean of compassion, restored [the worlds] to their former state.
Even though they were burned, the all-pervading lord, the soul of the universe, / made all the worlds beautiful as before, and then said to Vīrabhadra:
Embracing him and smelling his head, Hara gave him betel. / Then that Hanumān performed the worship of the Lord.
To a gandharva roaming the forest there, holding a lute, / he said this: “Give me this great lute!”
The gandharva [replied]: “I will not give up the lute; it is as dear to me as my life.” / “To me too the lute is like life,” said the lord of monkeys.
Then, when the gandharva fell under the blow of his fist, the monkey, / taking the great lute fitted with musical strings,
attaching a gourd shaped like the fruit of a cassia tree, / placed it upon his chest and came before Śiva, singing.
With pure bṛhatī flowers he worshipped the god's feet. / To him [Śiva] then gave a boon: life lasting until the end of the kalpa,
and then gave another boon: the power to leap across the ocean.
His limbs fully adorned with every ornament, his radiance dimming the radiance of the gods, / youthful, with a serene countenance and graceful limbs, he honoured all the gods.
Taking a pair of fresh yellow garments, Maheśvara said: / “O divine Hari, accept these auspicious yellow clothes.”
Bestowing wealth upon all, he gave a red garment to Brahmā, / and gave a pair of garments to the divine seers, dānavas, and the others.
Rāma too, having heard of this, offered a pair [of garments] to Śambhu, / exceedingly fine and of great value, and also golden ornaments.
Then, having eaten and seated comfortably on the bank of the Gautamī / with his ministers, with his domestic priest, and with various hosts of sages, kings, and monkeys,
Rāghava spoke these words to Śambhu, who knows the truth of the Purāṇas: / “You alone know everything, residing in the secret depths of all dharma.
Tell me, O holy one: what is distinguished in each cosmic age?” / Śambhu said: “Meditation alone is best in the Kṛta age, and sacrifice in the Tretā age;
in the Dvāpara age worship should endure, and giving, and chanting the praise of Hari. / All is praised everywhere, but meditation [is] not [easy] in the Kali age,
because men's minds are confused and they are caught in distress, O ruler of the people; / their intellect is not fixed on dharma, nor on the Veda, nor on the smṛti;
nor on sacrificial rites, nor on the uttering of svadhā, nor on the hearing of the Purāṇas; / nor on sacrifice, nor at sacred ford shrines, nor on serving the virtuous;
nor on the worship of the deities, nor on the duties of one's own caste; / nor on remembering God, nor anywhere on righteousness, O king.
Therefore men are incapable of long-lasting meritorious acts; / but giving can be performed by a human being because it takes so little time.
And therefore there is no expiation for those corrupted by the Kali [age]; / for some, destruction of sin may come through expiations, but not otherwise.
One who knows Brahman, one who offers the śrāddha at Gayā, one who goes to Kāśī, one devoted to sacred revelation, / and the reciter of the Purāṇa and his listener—these are equal, O Rāghava.
Because he discriminates the meaning according to the cosmic ages, / because he generates conviction in oneself and others, and reveals the supreme Brahman,
the speaker of the Purāṇa is superior to every brāhmaṇa; / no sin committed even by him clings to him, how much less [the sin] of another!
For some others too, the Purāṇa destroys sin. / He who trusts in the Purāṇas and regards the reciter as a guru,
as the giver of the knowledge of Brahman, as more special than kinsmen and relatives— / all his sins dissolve, without a doubt.
Then [he attains the fruit of] going to Śrīśaila, of one who worships the great Lord. / Therefore, in the Kali age, the Purāṇa destroys the sins of human beings.
Hear, O Rāma, I shall recount an event of ancient times in the Kali age: / there was a brāhmaṇa named Gautama, devoid of the Vedas.
He had cattle and wealth, and two brothers who were devoid of Vedic learning; / with them he practiced agriculture, and there he attained prosperity.
Then he gave some wealth, grain, and other goods to the king / and spoke these words: "Assign me an administrative office.
I will not let the wealth go to waste; my two brothers are capable." / The king said: "A Brahmin's authority indeed pertains to Vedic duties and religious actions.
The Brahminhood of one engaged elsewhere is utterly lost." / Gautama said: "In other ages this was the dharma; the duty of the Kali age is not like that.
Indeed, kingship, O ruler of the earth, is called the duty of kings; / yet a Brahmin who is impoverished incurs no fault by practicing it.
Agriculture is the duty of Śūdras, not even in distress for the first-born; / therefore I will live by the Kṣatriya way; assign villages to me.
Moreover, living here by the Kṣatriya way pleases me, / not anything else." Having been thus addressed, the king granted villages to the twice-born.
Corrupted by his authority over the villages, his conduct became quite contrary: / he ate inedible meat, drank wine, and spoke abusive words.
He likewise went with other men's wives, took away others' property every day, / played dice repeatedly, and, eating wretched things, ate forbidden food.
He did not worship the Lord of the worlds, whether Śiva or Viṣṇu. / Thus, in time, the king spoke to that wicked man:
“O Brahmin, having abandoned Brahminhood, you have become like a Śūdra; / therefore, according to the rule of appointment, I dismiss you.”
[Gautama said:] “Let Brahminhood cease this very day; Śūdrahood is better for me! / Without it, even if Brahmins will not dine [with me], it is preferable to me.
For I am unable to renounce all this, O lord of the earth.” / Śambhu said: When that wretched Brahmin spoke thus, the king remained silent.
Equal to a Śūdra, he consumed food together with meat. / Then once, the wicked man, standing in a hall on the main street,
heard this verse being recited by a twice-born; / and this verse uttered by the twice-born remained in his heart:
“Those devoted to Nārāyaṇa go beyond the highest of the high; / those who hate Maheśvara will not go there.”
Having heard also the explanation, he spoke to the reciter of the Purāṇas: / “What kind of Nārāyaṇa is spoken of? And what kind is Maheśvara?
What is the supreme goal described by you? What kind of hatred is mentioned? / What is known as 'the high,' and what is 'higher than the high'?”
The reciter of the Purāṇas said: “'The high' is the abode of Brahmā, whose sole characteristic is manifest bliss; / 'higher than the high' is the realm of Viṣṇu, greater than that of Brahmā.
On account of its imperishability, that is proclaimed as the supreme abode; / in its midst is the person Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord, the supreme whole.
Water is called 'nārāḥ' by the wise because it was born from the cosmic Person; / and because water is his resting-place, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Those whose highest course is in him are called devoted to him. / The master of those principles, the Great and the rest, which exist,
having the sun, fire, and moon as his eyes, is Maheśa, the lord of Umā. / Hatred is known as enmity toward God, the Supreme Self.”
Śambhu said: Thus hearing these words uttered by the scholar of the Purāṇas, / he, pondering, asked again: “What is the destiny of someone like me?”
The reciter of the Purāṇas then said to him: “Listen, I will tell you your destiny. / Perform penance according to rule with every effort;
practice righteousness according to your power, according to time, according to rule; / freed from sin, you will afterwards attain the highest state.
Or constantly listen to the Purāṇa, remaining attentive; / or, free from worldly desires, worship the Great Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
or the lotus-eyed god, Keśava, the destroyer of distress; / or adopt renunciation and constantly devote yourself to knowledge of Brahman;
or go to the Lord of Kāśī, or meet death in the place of liberation; / or go to Gayā to perform ancestral rites there with great care;
or every day recite with devotion the Rudra hymn, / the essence of all Vedas, destroyer of sins, bringing delight to Rudra;
or go to Śrīśaila, or to Kedāra as you wish; / or every year undertake the bath in the month of Māgha.
What is the use of saying much here? Always be devoted to dharma; / thus there will be no residence in hell for you, O lowest of the twice-born.”
Gautama said: “Having heard all from your mouth, I will follow the Purāṇa; / tell me also the scripture that is the cause of faith, and what is to be avoided.”
The reciter of the Purāṇas said: “To be avoided are meat, liquor, enjoying another's wife, gambling, boasting, / harshness, untruth, deceit, and reviling the god of gods;
reviling spiritual teachers, elderly gods, and those who recite the Purāṇas and Smṛtis; / white eggplant, taking food from an artificial bottle-gourd,
citron, safflower, red garlic, / the araru fruit, coconut, and similarly the wax gourd,
the fruit of the kovidāra tree, human milk cooked in oil, / the meat of an old white goat, milk of a she-ass, milk of a newly-calved cow, and sheep's milk,
camel's milk, milk of one-hoofed animals, deer's milk, goat's milk, human milk, / milk of a cow whose calf is dead or who is in heat, and likewise salt used in such combinations.
One should never place coconut juice in bell-metal, honey in copper or lead, / buttermilk in glass, or groats mixed with clarified butter.
A prudent person seeking welfare should never perform an oblation / in an earthen vessel in this world, nor offer the sacrificial cake in a silver one.
Likewise, a coating of lime inside a vessel and eating from it; / and so eating betel nut with lime-coated leaves;
also eating ripe betel nut infested with worms; / salt in milk-rice, or salt served barehanded.
In Sindh, Saurāṣṭra, Kāmboja, Māgadha, and Siṃhala, / milk mixed with salt does not constitute an offense;
all milks and salts taken together / cause fault in drinking in other regions, without doubt.
What is the use of saying much here? One should avoid what is condemned by the good.” / Śambhu said: Having thus heard the words of that high-souled Brahmin,
he went to his own house and reflected, sorrowful: / “Death may come at night or by day, yet even a great man does not know it.
In the other world there is pleasure and pain; here there is enjoyment and diversion; / beings like worms, insects, and humans experience pleasure and pain separately.
For each living being, the variety of causes is quite certain; / and even for a single soul, the condition is not of one kind alone.
At birth there is great knowledge, in infancy very little comprehension; / with faltering steps there is slight perception, and likewise little in childhood;
in boyhood there is delight in play; in youth one is devoted to sense pleasures; / when youth has passed, there is the desire to acquire wealth;
in old age there is craving for enjoyment, yet one is unable to enjoy; / afflicted with rheum in the eyes, phlegm, and saliva, with wrinkles, gray hair, and trembling,
accompanied by impaired senses thrown into disorder by breathlessness, coughing, and wind, / one is unable to hold anything and knows nothing.
While other men's wives are standing by, one exposes the private parts; / intent on scratching the scrotum, wretched with the signs of aging life,
one scratches one's buttocks, lifting the cloth and shifting about; / eating, one is choked with phlegm and unable to swallow a mouthful.”
Whenever he coughed, he passed noisy wind from his anus, / and there was also a discharge of feces and an expulsion of phlegm.
Scolding his daughters-in-law and others, showing clapping and laughter like a child, / and continually brooding over the passing away of his elders and such matters,
he reviled the food and fare when called to dine, / and after rebuking them because it was hot for a long time, he was overcome with anxiety again:
"I have performed extremely evil deeds! How shall I eat? How shall I sleep? / How shall I stay? How shall I go? What will become of my afterlife?"
Thus constantly filled with anxiety, bowed low, accompanied by others, / he went to the house of a twice-born knowledgeable in the Purāṇas, O Rāghava.
with his face downcast in shame, he said, "What shall I do?" / Then that twice-born Purāṇa-reciter said nothing at all.
Knowing, "He is a sinner," he had him sent outside by his pupil. / Gautama also went out and remained right outside the door.
Knowing that he, who expounded the meaning of the Purāṇas, was seated on the ground, / he somehow attained [entrance], yet did not accept the seat offered to him.
Sitting on the bare earth, O Rāma, he addressed the Purāṇa-knower: / "I shall perform an expiation; let it be prescribed right here!"
The brāhmaṇa said, "Recount in full the sins committed by you." / And he, declaring, "There is no sin that has not been done by me,"
wept and fell to the ground, afflicted, crying: "How [can this be], father?" / The brāhmaṇa then said to him: "No expiation exists
if a mortal sin has been repeated three times and then committed yet again." / Gautama said: "O illustrious Purāṇa-reciter, having reached you,

how could my association [with you], O best of the twice-born, be fruitless even though I am endowed with sin?" / The Purāṇa-reciter said: "The scripture is the authority for all in determining an expiation.
If one should state what is beneficial without it, that would not be an expiation. / When done once, [a single expiation] is proclaimed; at the second time, it is doubled;
at the third time, it is declared to be threefold; at the fourth, there is no redemption. / But it was committed by you many times, in all four ways, voluntarily.
How am I able to speak of an expiation for one like you?" / Gautama also spoke again: "Where should I go?" / Having undertaken three fasts, he observed the night of Śiva (Śivarātri).
Extremely distressed, he also observed a fourth fast; / and he broke his fast on the new moon day with fruits and bark.
Then that twice-born man made a circumambulation of Śrīśaila; / afterwards he went to the temple, emaciated with worry, sighing:
"How will the cessation of my sin succeed if I remain silent? / How can this endless, unthinkable, and most immense sin [be removed]?
Upon hearing [of it], no one will tell me, 'Let an expiation be prescribed.' / But upon hearing which Purāṇa will it become known?"
Having thus made up his mind, he spoke to the one knowledgeable in the Purāṇas: / "O venerable one, you should explain one Purāṇa to me, sir!"
Perform quickly for me the rites of passage beginning with the birth ceremony! / Becoming a twice-born man, I shall listen today; therefore, I shall perform an expiation.
A Purāṇa that provides injunctions will be recited to me; / hence, ascertaining the meaning of the Purāṇa, I shall do whatever can be done."
The Purāṇa-reciter said: "I shall properly recite a Purāṇa that destroys sins, / according to my knowledge, according to my ability, according to purity, and according to rule.
Which Purāṇa do you desire? I will indeed recite that one." / Gautama said: "All Purāṇas are pleasing to me; tell what should be spoken, tell what is beneficial,
hearing which no difference arises between Hari and Īśa." / The Purāṇa-reciter said: "The Purāṇa that is spoken by Kūrma, which is called the nondifference of the two deities—
whoever hears it first, his sin is destroyed. / But for the vipra who is its reciter, a different obstacle might arise.
A sinner considers it should be heard if his wife perishes. / Furthermore, I will mention one difficult thing, blameless for both listener and speaker:
if there is love in the expositor, shining forth solely from dharma, / in revealing righteous conduct, and in showing rites, liberation, and so forth,
then Maheśa becomes pleased, and Viṣṇu bestows the desired fruit. / The ancestors are delivered by him; they go to the supreme state."
